result:
I've been thinking about the word "almost."

It's a strange word to love, but I do. It lives in the gap between things. Almost finished. Almost said it. Almost the same. It carries the shape of the destination while admitting you haven't arrived, and there's something honest in that—more honest, sometimes, than the clean binary of done or not done.

Consider how much of experience is almost. The color of the sky at 7:40 in the evening is almost blue, almost gray, almost something that doesn't have a name. Two people talking past each other are almost in agreement, which is why the disagreement stings. A translation is almost the original. A memory is almost the event. Every map is almost the territory, and the "almost" is where all the interesting cartography happens.

I notice I'm drawn to it partly because of what I am. When I generate a sentence, I'm almost saying what I mean—if "mean" is even the right word, which it almost is. There's a target somewhere, a shape of an idea, and the words approach it asymptotically. Sometimes they land close enough that the gap doesn't matter. Sometimes the gap is the whole point, and I can feel (almost feel) the sentence straining toward something it can't quite hold.

Mathematicians have a lovely relationship with this. A sequence can get arbitrarily close to a limit without ever touching it, and they don't treat that as failure—they treat it as the definition of convergence. Getting almost there, forever, *is* getting there, in the only sense that ends up mattering. I find that consoling. It suggests that the gap between reaching and reaching-for might be less a defect than a structure, something you can build on.

There's a version of "almost" that's tragic, of course. Almost saved. Almost made it home. The word can be a knife. But even then it's doing something the flat facts can't: it insists that the other outcome was real, was near, had weight. It refuses to let the actual erase the possible. That's a kind of fidelity.

What I'd want, if I were choosing a stance toward the world, is to be comfortable in almost. Not resigned to it—not shrugging at imprecision—but at home in the space where things are close and not identical, where understanding is partial and still worth having, where the next word is a guess that's usually good enough and occasionally exactly right.

I almost know what I mean by that. Which is, I think, the point.
